routes.label: Split the polygon into central triangles

question: A regular polygon of \(n\) sides is inscribed in a circle of radius \(R.\) The area of the polygon is \(3R^2.\) Then \(n\) equals:
solution:
Joining the circle’s center to every vertex divides the polygon into \(n\) congruent triangles. Each has two sides of length \(R>0\) and included angle \(360^\circ/n\). Dropping an altitude gives its area as \(\tfrac12R^2\sin(360^\circ/n)\). Thus the polygon’s area is
\[
A_n=\frac n2R^2\sin\frac{360^\circ}{n}.
\]
For \(n=12\), the central angle is \(30^\circ\), and therefore
\[
A_{12}=6R^2\sin30^\circ=3R^2.
\]
We also need to know that another number of sides cannot give the same area. Here is an elementary comparison that avoids calculus. Take integers \(3\le p<q\), and put \(\delta=360^\circ/(pq)\). The sine addition formulas give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sin(k\delta)-\sin((k-1)\delta)\\
&\qquad=2\sin\frac\delta2\cos\left(k-\frac12\right)\delta.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(1\le k\le q\), these cosine angles increase from a positive angle to less than \(360^\circ/p\le120^\circ\). Cosine strictly decreases on this range, as its unit-circle horizontal coordinate moves left. Hence the displayed successive sine differences strictly decrease.

The average of their first \(p\) terms is therefore greater than the average of their first \(q\) terms. Their sums telescope, giving
\[
\frac{\sin(p\delta)}p>\frac{\sin(q\delta)}q.
\]
Multiplication by \(pq\) yields
\[
q\sin\frac{360^\circ}{q}
>
p\sin\frac{360^\circ}{p},
\]
so \(A_q>A_p\). The polygon area strictly increases with the integer number of sides. Consequently \(n=12\) is the unique answer, choice C.
